Veterans say they were effectively used as test subjects, with some exposed to radioactive fallout without adequate protection.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced an independent inquiry into the impact of Britain’s Cold War nuclear weapons tests on military veterans and their families.

In a statement, the prime minister said: "Nuclear test veterans and their families have waited too long for the truth, and that’s exactly what the independent panel will establish."

Around 22,000 British service personnel witnessed nuclear tests in the Indian and Pacific oceans between 1952 and 1967. Many of those affected say they felt they were used as test subjects, with some exposed to radioactive fallout without adequate protection.

Veterans and their families have campaigned for recognition and compensation for around 40 years, linking the tests to illnesses affecting both participants and, in some cases, their children.

Campaigners met the prime minister at an event at 10 Downing Street. It came a day after the BBC aired a special edition of Newsnight on Tuesday, in which some surviving veterans shared their experiences.

Britain's nuclear tests

The UK's first atmospheric atomic test took place on 3 October 1952, when a plutonium implosion device was detonated near the Montebello Islands off Western Australia.

Dozens more nuclear explosions were carried out by the UK in Australia and Pacific territories, including Kiritimati, formerly known as Christmas Island.

Campaigners say many military personnel were exposed to nuclear fallout after being ordered to fly through mushroom clouds or witness explosions without protective equipment.

Unlike the United States and France, the UK has no dedicated compensation scheme for nuclear test veterans.

Britain's Ministry of Defence has said there was no evidence that Britain’s nuclear tests had caused increased health risks, citing four studies as well as research by Brunel University in 2022.

However, veterans and campaigners have accused the MoD of withholding complete medical records, including blood and urine test results, which they argue could help establish a link between radiation exposure and illness later in life.

The MoD released some official documents in July 2026, but said some records may have been inadvertently destroyed three years earlier.

An independent panel will take on the investigation

The British government says the panel will be modelled on the Hillsborough Independent Panel, rather than being a conventional statutory public inquiry. It says this should allow for a faster, more collaborative process, with veterans and their families closely involved.

The government says the panel's terms of reference are likely to include the conditions servicemen were exposed to, what the state knew and when, advice given to ministers and statements made to Parliament, as well as how veterans and their health concerns were handled.

The panel is expected to deliver an interim report by 3 October 2027, the 75th anniversary of Britain's first nuclear weapons test.

Andy Burnham said his government would also pursue memorialisation, education and research alongside the inquiry, rather than waiting for its final conclusions.

A national memorial service is being planned for 3 October 2027.

The EU is preparing a voluntary agreement to accelerate data centre expansion as it seeks to triple capacity within five to seven years, despite growing concerns about electricity consumption and pressure on power grids.

A leaked European Commission draft accessed by Euronews reveals that the EU wants national governments, operators and energy companies to agree on measures to make new data centres easier to build and connect to electricity networks.

But rather than imposing binding sustainability requirements, the Commission is proposing a framework countries can adapt to their needs.

The document, "EU model for tripartite agreements on the sustainable integration of data centres into the energy system", describes the proposed commitments as a "toolbox rather than a single integrated package that needs to be adopted as such".

Countries could pick and choose measures covering grid access, renewable energy, storage, flexibility and the reuse of excess heat from data centres to warm buildings. Crucially, the draft states that "participation in local tripartite agreements is voluntary" and that the commitments "do not create any legal obligations for the signatory parties".

In parallel, Brussels is developing separate rules and standards to improve data centres' sustainability, raising questions about their compatibility with voluntary industry participation.

Europe's growing appetite for data centres

Data centres are facilities packed with servers that store, process and transmit digital information. They power everything from online banking and cloud services to AI, which demands huge computing capacity.

The leaked draft puts the EU's installed data centre capacity at approximately 12 gigawatts in 2025. According to International Energy Agency estimates, capacity stood at around 52 gigawatts in the US and 28 gigawatts in China that year.

The Commission sees expanding capacity as key to digital sovereignty. But MEP Benedetta Scuderi questioned whether this would strengthen Europe's autonomy, particularly if new infrastructure is developed by American technology companies.

"We know that we have very scarce resources for building data centres: energy, water and land. We need to be sure that what we build is what we need, that we don't go beyond that, that these data centres are not oversized or unnecessarily large-scale, and that they support our digital sovereignty. We cannot sell out our natural resources to American Big Tech because that would be of no benefit to us."

Data centres require huge supplies of electricity and cooling systems that can consume vast amounts of water. According to the Commission's draft, they already account for around 2.5% of EU electricity consumption, while their concentration near major hubs is increasing pressure on local grids.

That challenges Europe's energy transition, which also requires electricity for transport, buildings and industrial decarbonisation.

The draft's plans for centres and member states

The Commission is trying to balance these priorities through several energy and digital policy initiatives, including the Cloud and AI Development Act. Existing EU environmental and energy-efficiency rules already require data centres to report on sustainability, including energy efficiency and water use.

The leaked draft also mentions a common EU sustainability rating scheme to make facilities' environmental performance easier to compare. It proposes a collaborative approach through tripartite agreements, bringing together public authorities, data centre operators and energy companies to negotiate arrangements for individual projects or broader national and regional development plans.

According to the draft, the aim is to support "faster rollout of data centre projects, improve their visibility, improve local acceptance, and add value to the energy system and the community".

For member states, this could mean designating areas for new data centres based on grid capacity, environmental factors and opportunities to reuse excess heat. Authorities would also be encouraged to coordinate electricity, heating and digital infrastructure planning, streamline grid connections and prevent speculative projects from hogging scarce capacity. The draft suggests checking whether projects have permits, financing and sufficient technical readiness before granting grid access.

Data centre operators would share electricity demand forecasts and project updates with grid operators and consider flexible connection agreements. These could speed up grid access in exchange for limiting electricity consumption at certain times. Operators would also be encouraged to invest in clean power, sign long-term power purchase agreements and shift computing workloads to periods when electricity is more readily available.

Waste heat is another major focus, as heat generated by servers could be recovered to warm homes, schools and hospitals through district heating networks. The draft encourages operators to publish heat-reuse readiness plans, explore connections to local heating networks and negotiate long-term commercial deals where feasible. Governments could help through infrastructure planning, heat purchase agreements for public buildings and funding to cover upfront costs.

Voluntary commitments versus environmental ambitions

The proposed framework does not require every new facility to finance enough additional renewable energy to cover its consumption. Instead, it proposes that member states "explore options for pursuing the time matching of clean energy supply" with data centre demand, leaving the intervals, shares and implementation timelines to national authorities.

Scuderi warned of the consequences of increasing electricity demand in already strained energy systems.

"If you put a huge increase in electricity demand on an already pressured electricity system, what will happen is that we will have a collapse of the system. We will have a huge increase in prices, and we will not know where to get electricity for things that are strategic, such as industry and households.

"When you are asking for a certain number of megawatts for a data centre, we need to know where we're getting this electricity. This needs to come mostly from renewable energy.

"We need to require data centres to produce a certain amount of renewable energy, and the increase in the number of data centres needs to be sustainable in terms of electricity production, without an increase in emissions and without relying on fossil fuel-based electricity production."

While the EU's Energy Efficiency Directive already contains requirements for assessing waste-heat recovery opportunities, the draft's additional commitments would remain voluntary.

It also allows for commercial and technical constraints: where no heat recovery agreement is reached, operators could proceed with facilities designed to accommodate future heat exports. The framework would encourage earlier planning and cooperation without guaranteeing that recoverable heat will reach nearby communities.

While the document presents sustainability as a central objective, it also explicitly seeks to make data centre development faster and more predictable.

The Commission's role

Despite the voluntary nature of the agreements, the Commission plans to retain a central coordinating role, having developed the model with input from authorities in 18 member states and 14 industry associations representing data centres, electricity networks, renewables and storage.

The first local agreements could begin in 2027, potentially alongside data centre acceleration zones under the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act. Brussels would monitor progress annually until at least 2035, share best practices and regularly update the Energy Council and, where appropriate, the European Parliament.

Taylor died "following a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", the band announced.

British synth pop-rockers Duran Duran have paid tribute to their guitarist Andy Taylor, who has died at the age of 65.

In a joint statement the band and Taylor’s family announced that Taylor had died “following a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer”. The statement added that he “passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday November 23, 2026”.

“To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,” shared Taylor’s wife Tracey on behalf of the family. “He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home."

“Andy faced the last few years with so much courage and determination. He never gave up, fighting until the very end, never losing his love of life. The kindness and support shown to him by fans from all over the world throughout his illness brought him immense comfort and strength, and for that we will always be grateful."

She added: “Andy knew just how deeply he was loved, and we take great comfort in that. We will miss him every single day.”

View this post on Instagram

Meanwhile, Taylor’s former Duran Duran bandmates honoured his work across hit songs such as ‘Hungry Like The Wolf’, ‘The Wild Boys’, ‘Rio’ and the James Bond theme 'A View To A Kill’.

“Andy was there at the very beginning of our story,” the band shared. “From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."

“It was great to make music with him again when the original five reunited in the early 2000s, and that time together, both on stage and in the studio, meant a tremendous amount to all of us. When we were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, Andy was too unwell to join us, but his words that night reminded everyone of his strength and the bond we shared.”

The band continued: “Andy faced his illness with remarkable courage, honesty and grace. Our thoughts are with his wife Tracey, his children Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew, and grandson Albie. They all loved him deeply and we ask that their privacy be respected at this very difficult time. In lieu of flowers, the family has asked that donations be made in Andy’s name to Prostate Cancer UK. With love from Simon, John, Nick and Roger.”

Duran Duran members also shared individual statements on their website, with frontman Simon Le Bon remembering “the blond bombshell, firebrand teenager I met in 1980″.

“He’s the kid from the Northeast who can really play guitar,” he recalled. “If you like, he can play it like Mick Ronson, or he can play it like Jimmy Page, he can even play rinky-dink rhythm like Nile Rodgers. But what he does most is play guitar like guitar-genius – Andy Taylor! He came fresh off touring Army bases in West Germany. Spikey hair and spikey personality. Andy didn’t mince his words; he didn’t suffer fools gladly. Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive, overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later when his own life is cut so short.”

Le Bon concluded: “There’s a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart. It’ll never close up; I won’t let it. I will miss him and love him for all my days.”

Born in Tynemouth in Northumberland in 1961, Taylor began playing guitar age 11 when he was tutored by Dave Black from Bowie’s Spiders From Mars. He would join Duran Duran in 1980 after they advertised for a guitarist in Melody Maker.

Taylor was also a member of The Power Station with Robert Palmer and worked as guitarist, songwriter, and record producer with the likes of Rod Stewart and Belinda Carlisle.

Taylor revealed that he had been battling stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years on the night he was inducted in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022. He was unable to attend the event and said: “I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band. You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one’s own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible.”

Taylor published his memoir "Wild Boy: My Life In Duran Duran" in 2008.

He is survived by his wife Tracey Wilson, and their four children Andrew, Georgina, Bethany and Isabella.

UniCredit has also obtained the final regulatory clearance needed to press ahead with the public takeover and exchange offer for Commerzbank. On 26 November the Polish financial supervisory authority (KNF) approved the transaction, completing the approval process required for the acquisition of the German bank. The green light from Warsaw was the last missing piece after authorisations from the European Commission and the US Federal Reserve.

The Polish approval specifically concerns the indirect change of control of Commerzbank's operations in Poland, including mBank, in which the German group holds 69.1 per cent. It is one of the country's main banking institutions, with around 5.9 million customers, and is also active in mortgages, investment and payments.

KNF authorisation was necessary because the acquisition of Commerzbank also entails UniCredit taking control of its Polish subsidiaries. Banking rules stipulate that a change of control of the parent company must be reviewed by the supervisory authorities also with regard to qualified indirect holdings in its subsidiaries.

The approval process and the agreement with Berlin

The Polish green light comes after that of the European Commission, which on 16 November cleared the deal unconditionally from a competition standpoint. Brussels assessed the impact of integrating Commerzbank and HypoVereinsbank (HVB), UniCredit's German subsidiary, and ruled out negative effects on the market. Authorisation from the Federal Reserve was granted in the same period.

On the political front, a decisive step was the agreement reached in mid-November between UniCredit's chief executive, Andrea Orcel, and the German government. To overcome Berlin's resistance, the Italian group made eight binding commitments regarding the bank's industrial and employment prospects and the preservation of a strong presence in Germany.

The guarantees include the central role of Frankfurt as the base for German operations, the retention of Commerzbank's stock market listing and its legal form as a German joint-stock company. UniCredit has also pledged to ensure adequate representation of Commerzbank and HypoVereinsbank on the group's executive committee and to propose the appointment of German nationals to its own board of directors when it is renewed in 2027.

The other commitments concern support for German small and medium-sized enterprises, the so-called Mittelstand, through UniCredit's international network, the appropriate allocation of capital and decision-making autonomy for operations in Germany. Investment in Frankfurt is also planned in training, digital technologies and artificial intelligence, along with continued dialogue with trade unions and protection of existing agreements for employees.

The issue of the German state's stake

The question of the state's stake in Commerzbank remains open. The German government holds about 13.3 per cent of the share capital through the SoFFin stabilisation fund and had already announced in June that it would not take part in UniCredit's offer by tendering its shares.

Berlin has not so far announced an immediate sale of its stake. The state's presence in the shareholding structure is also a way to monitor developments in the transaction closely and to verify that UniCredit honours its commitments, particularly on governance, employment and Germany's role in the group's activities.

Next steps

With the completion of regulatory approvals, the deal can now move on to the next stages of implementation. The crediting of the new shares to the custodian banks is scheduled to take place by 7 December 2026.

UniCredit has also asked Commerzbank to call an extraordinary general meeting to elect a new board of directors. This step is part of the process of defining the future governance of the German bank.

For UniCredit, the transaction implies an estimated capital absorption of between 200 and 225 basis points of CET1, the main indicator of a bank's capital strength, in return for a significant expected contribution to the group's profits.

Greece's Ministry of Health is moving ahead with plans to launch specialised services for people with Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.

The aim of these programmes is to preserve the cognitive and functional abilities of people with dementia, strengthen their autonomy and improve their daily functioning.

They also aim to prevent or delay the worsening of symptoms, reduce social isolation and avoid early institutionalisation. The extended opening hours of the facilities are expected to make it easier for patients and their families to access the services.

Meanwhile, the mobile units will provide home care, particularly in cases where it is difficult or impossible for patients to travel to the centres.

The new facilities will also offer support for family carers, who shoulder much of the day-to-day care of people with dementia. They can access counselling services, psychological support and training programmes to help them manage caregiving demands.

The development of these services is particularly important, as dementia affects not only those who are ill, but also their family and social environment. The growing need for care, combined with an ageing population, makes it necessary to create facilities that provide stable, specialised and accessible support.

"Dementia does not concern only the person who is ill, but also their family, their carers and society as a whole," Vartzopoulos said. "The state must stand by them, with high-quality and free services, with respect for the dignity and autonomy of every person".

The new centres will be launched across Greece, with particular emphasis on strengthening regional coverage and reducing inequalities in access to specialised mental health services.

The inventory of Antoni Gaudí's estate reveals that the legendary Spanish architect wished to devote all his assets, including his Parc Güell house and his savings, to financing the works of the iconic Sagrada Família.

The inventory of Antoni Gaudí's estate has been revealed a century after his death and it shows the architect's deep committment to the Sagrada Familia. His last wish was to dedicate all his assets, from his savings to his home in Parc Güell, to financing the construction of the temple.

The document, kept in the Arxiu Històric de Protocols de Barcelona, is a 1926 copy of the will that Gaudí signed in 1911 in Puigcerdà. The original disappeared in 1936, after the notary's office that held it burned down in the first months of the Civil War. Among the papers is also the certificate of last wills signed by Manuel Azaña, then a Justice official and future president of the Second Republic.

As the dean of the Col·legi Notarial de Catalunya, José Alberto Marín, has explained, notarial documents are subject to protocol secrecy, but they are considered historical records and become open to public consultation once 100 years have passed.

An inheritance in the service of the Sagrada Familia

The inventory makes it possible to identify the three trusted heirs appointed by Gaudí, a figure specific to Catalan succession law. They were the priest Gil Parés i Vilasau, chaplain custodian of the Sagrada Familia; the doctor Pere Santaló i Castellví, a close friend of the architect; and Domènec Sugrañes i Gras, an architect and Gaudí's disciple who would later take over the direction of the works on the temple.

The three appeared before notary Luis Rufasta and recorded that Gaudí's express wish was to sell all his assets and hand over the money raised to the construction of the basilica. Sugrañes acted in place of Francesc Berenguer i Mestres, a close collaborator of the architect who had died in 1914.

A modest fortune and a single property

The inventory shows the austerity with which Gaudí lived in his final years. His savings were split between two bank accounts: one with 1,870 pesetas at the Banco de España in Barcelona, and another with 1,121 pesetas in a savings book at Caixa de Pensions per a la Vellesa i d'Estalvis.

His only property was the house in Parc Güell, in the former municipality of Gràcia, which the executors valued at 45,000 pesetas for the purposes of a possible sale. According to estimates by the Col·legi Notarial de Catalunya, that sum would be equivalent today to around €150,000 and represented an ordinary level of wealth for the time.

The documents confirm Gaudí's limited attachment to material possessions and his determination to put all his resources at the service of the project to which he devoted much of his life.

A document of particular historical value

The significance of the inventory goes beyond its financial content. The destruction of the original will in 1936 made this copy a key piece for reconstructing the architect's last wishes. In addition, the presence of Manuel Azaña's signature gives the document an element of particular historical interest.

After the legal period of 100 years has elapsed, the inventory will be available for consultation at the premises of the Col·legi Notarial de Catalunya, which has so far kept it in the Arxiu Històric de Protocols de Barcelona.

The archive also holds other documents linked to Gaudí and the Sagrada Familia, including the record of the laying of the basilica's first stone, signed before the architect took over the direction of the works.

Among its most recent holdings is also the document signed in June this year by the Pope Leo XIV and the Archbishop of Barcelona, Joan Josep Omella, which records the completion of the Tower of Jesus and the state of the works on the temple.

EU leaders are set to clash over the next EU budget and future support for Ukraine at a crucial summit in Brussels.

The stage is set for a tense summit in Brussels where EU leaders will spar over the size of the next budget and future support for Ukraine.

On the table are two proposals.

The first, by European Council President António Costa, is a seven-year budget worth almost €1.7 trillion, which some leaders say is too much and others say is too little.

The second, by the European Commission, is a €45 billion support loan for Ukraine, financed through joint debt. Three countries – Slovakia, Hungary and the Czech Republic – want to opt out of the loan, infuriating Kyiv's bilateral donors.

Although the budget and the loan are technically separate, they have become politically intertwined, creating a potentially volatile mix. After all, they are both about money.

"Now it's time for all of the leaders participating in this debate with an open mind, a constructive approach in the sense of compromise, because we need to approve this budget (by) the end of this year," Costa said on Thursday morning.

Also up for discussion is the succession of Christine Lagarde at the helm of the European Central Bank. Spain's candidate, Pablo Hernández de Cos, has taken the lead over Klaas Knot from the Netherlands and is widely tipped to snatch the top job.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has criticised the European Commission's proposed package of sanctions against Russia, which, among other measures, targets Russian sports figures.

"We are going too far in politicising sporting and cultural events in this way,'" he said as he arrived at a European Council summit focused on support for Ukraine and the EU's next long-term budget.

The European Commission unveiled its latest sanctions package against Russia last Thursday, proposing to ban Russian sports teams and athletes competing under the Russian flag, as well as the display of official Russian symbols, from all sporting events inside the bloc.

It also wants to ban Russian nationals from making financial donations to, or holding positions within, governing bodies of European-based sports federations.

"Sports events can not be a forum for propaganda activities," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said last week when unveiling the latest package — the 22nd since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Brussels aims for a deal on the latest sanctions package in December before the Christmas break.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal has warned that Ukraine faces a winter "like hell" and urged the EU to maintain its support for Kyiv.

Leaders at the EU summit will discuss how to fill the funding gap for Ukraine, but four member states – Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Bulgaria – have signalled they will not take part in a joint loan.

"Ukraine will probably face a winter that is like hell. They must know that Europe has their back in terms of money. We must decide on Ukraine funding," Michal said, adding that the EU should not cut its defence spending in the next budgetary period.

The prime minister said Estonia's border closure with Russia, which takes effect next week, will boost European security.

"You cannot tolerate attacks on NATO territory, against the defence industry. And Russia has the special services, filtering everybody who crosses the border and taking advantage of that information. So that increases the security of Europe, that we close the east border."

Estonia decided to close the border for six months in response to a wave of Russia-linked hybrid attacks targeting Estonian defence companies.

Latvia's PM Andris Kulbergs has warned that high energy costs and excessive bureaucracy are undermining the bloc’s – and represent a key obstacle to reaching a deal on the EU’s next long-term budget.

“The biggest problem is economy,” Kulbergs said, pointing to weak growth as a source of wider instability across Europe.

The Latvian leader said the budget must be concluded this year, given the urgent demands created by the war in Ukraine and the bloc's growing security and defence needs.

However, Kulbergs added that the negotiations are taking place against a backdrop of economic stagnation and political discontent.

Bulgaria will join Ukraine loan but not its military strand, Bulgarian PM says

Bulgaria will not seek a blank opt-out of the new €45 billion support loan to Ukraine after all, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev confirmed on Thursday morning. Radev had previously said Bulgaria would not take part in the scheme.

Instead, the country will remove itself from the military strand (€25 billion) and only take part in the financial strand (€20 billion).

"We have a huge historical diaspora of 300,000 Bulgarians living in Ukraine. And our wishes and our request (are) to concentrate our support in the areas of the Bulgarian population in Ukraine," Radev said.

"So we are going to contribute, but again, no money from Bulgaria for weapons, no money for war in Ukraine."

Radev says he will discuss the issue with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who presented the loan last week. Von der Leyen said member states with reservations about military support could opt in only to the financial side of the scheme.

Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs accused the EU of failing to deliver a level playing field for farmers, arguing that the bloc’s next long-term budget risks entrenching splits in agricultural aid between member states.

"If it does not do so, it means that there are political motives, rather than economic ones, behind our accession to the eurozone," he said as he arrived at Thursday's European Council summit, which is focusing on the bloc's long-term budget.

"How is it that the Commission has only now realised that budgetary funds in Bulgaria are being spent indiscriminately, without the necessary oversight?"

"How is it that inflation in Bulgaria suddenly fell in April to May last year?"

Radev previously described the Commission's warning as a "stinging rebuke" of previous governments' public spending policies.

Nausėda insisted the EU as a whole should support Kyiv, because the Ukrainians are not just fighting for their freedom but for the freedom of the whole of Europe.

“Ukraine could and should negotiate from the strongest side. If they feel this deficit of financial resources or military equipment, of course, the Russian Federation will be in a better position to start negotiations,” he continued.

"We remember that there was support in Europe when it was about migration. And now it's the eastern flank's turn, because we are the ones defending the EU's border," Kulbergs said.

"The Baltics need to get the support to get our economy up to speed, so we can allocate resources for defence."

Cohesion and supporting Ukraine are both about solidarity, Lithuania’s President says

“For me, both issues are a matter of solidarity. First, the solidarity with Ukraine and the second, solidarity within the European Union,” said the President of Lithuania, Gitanas Nausėda.

For the Lithuanian leader, Costa’s proposal on the EU budget is a very good starting point for the leaders’ discussion. Still, he criticised the cuts to the Connecting Europe facility, the funding program for infrastructural projects.

“What disappoints me a bit, of course, is the reduction of national envelopes. My country has not completed the conversion process. We are at 90% of the European Union average. Our farmers receive only about 80% of direct payments of European Union average,” he said.

For Nausėda, it is also not fair that regions in the far north of the bloc receive additional financial support, while that is not the case for the regions at the eastern border despite the daily threats from Russia and spillovers from the war in Ukraine.

Black Sea security to feature in EU talks as Romania warns of wider regional risks

Black Sea security will be raised during the talks as Romania seeks to keep the strategic importance of the region high on the European agenda amid the war in Ukraine, the country's President Nicușor Dan told reporters.

Dan said the issue would feature in informal discussions with other EU leaders, following a dedicated session on Black Sea security at NATO.

“Black Sea security will also be raised,” Dan said, adding that the issue continued to feature in discussions with Romania’s allies within the Alliance.

The remarks underline how the war in Ukraine has placed the Black Sea at the centre of European security concerns, with the conflict carrying risks beyond Ukraine’s borders.

Romania borders the Black Sea and sees the region’s security closely tied to the outcome of the war and the broader relationship between Russia and NATO.

Costa calls on leaders to have 'open mind' and 'compromise' on EU budget

European Council President António Costa, the moderator-in-chief of today's talks, has urged the 27 leaders to have an "open mind" and move beyond their red lines on the EU budget. Costa has tabled a revised proposal worth €1.7 trillion for seven years.

"Now it's time for all of the leaders participating in this debate with an open mind, a constructive approach in the sense of compromise, because we need to approve this budget (in time). That means by the end of this year, and for this, we need to reach unanimity," Costa told reporters upon arrival.

"The European budget is not like the national budget. It's enough to have a majority now. We need unanimity, and to have the unanimity, all the leaders need to listen to each other, taking into account the positions of the others in order to have a common landing zone."

Costa says he aims to bring leaders "closer" on three main areas: the overall size of the budget, the distribution of its priorities, and the package of EU-wide taxes, also known as "new own resources".

"We need the long-term budget fit to fund our main priorities. We need to support our farmers. We need to support our cities and regions. We need to invest more in security, in defence. We need to boost competitiveness, and we need to answer to the expectations of our citizens," he said.

Costa will wait until the end of the day to decide whether the summit should continue on Friday.

The collapse of Poundland marks another major setback for Britain's struggling retail sector, which has been hit by weak consumer spending, rising costs and fierce competition.

Struggling UK discounter Poundland fell into administration on Wednesday, its American owner announced, putting at risk around 11,000 jobs and 600 stores.

"The news that it has gone into administration just weeks before Christmas will be deeply concerning for workers and their families," British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement.

Poundland's owner Gordon Brothers earlier announced it had appointed administrators AlixPartners to try and save parts of the business.

"Efforts to preserve as many jobs and stores as possible will continue, led by the administrators," the US investment firm said in a statement.

Business consultancy firm AlixPartners said its "priority... is to work with all stakeholders", including the UK government and unions, "as we identify the best possible route forward".

"We would encourage anybody interested in acquiring the business in part or as a whole... to contact the administrators," added an AlixPartners spokesperson.

Retail trade union Usdaw accused Gordon Brothers of failing to engage with the body, adding that the fall into administration was "devastating news" for its members in the runup to Christmas.

Gordon Brothers had taken control of Poundland only in June last year, providing £85 million (€97 million) in financing to help turn around its fortunes, while shutting shops and axing staff.

Previous owner, Polish discounter Pepco Group, had said that the already-struggling business faced added pressure from a business-tax rise in the UK.

It was sold to Gordon Brothers for £1, with a portfolio of more than 800 stores.

Poundland and other discounters came to the fore in Britain following the 2008 global financial crisis, providing consumers with everyday essentials at knockdown prices.

However, they have struggled to compete in recent years owing to high inflation and increased competition from supermarkets.

"Supported by Gordon Brothers, the management team and colleagues at Poundland worked hard over the past 12 months to improve the underlying performance and achieve £100 million of cost savings," the owner added in Wednesday's statement.

"Despite a reduced cost base, looking forward, the business is still vulnerable to inflationary pressures or any downturn in sales and margin," it added.

AlixPartners said Poundland will continue to trade as normal as it explores ways to keep at least part of the business running.

From Pacific island nations where flights come weekly to a little-visited part of Europe, here’s where to head when you’re looking to visit a place none of your friends have been.

As destinations battle overtourism, more and more of us are seeking out alternatives or “hidden gems”.

Some 102 million tourists made it to France, the world’s most-visited country, in 2025, so your odds of finding some unknown spot there are pretty unlikely.

But what about a country where the number of tourists doesn’t even hit 3,500 annually, or a European nation where tourist arrivals aren’t yet six figures?

Here, we’ve rounded up 13 of the least-visited countries around the world, and detailed how to get there from Europe.

NB: For obvious reasons, we’ve excluded countries that have travel advisories in place, like Sudan or Somalia, so this might not be the definitive list of least-visited countries.

Tuvalu

Officially the least visited country in the world, just 3,136 tourists made it to Tuvalu’s shores in 2023, according to the country’s Central Statistics Division.

If you want to count yourself among them, you’ll need to act fast, as the low-lying Pacific island nation is predicted to be 95% submerged as a result of rising sea levels by 2100.

As for what to do here, there are no real surprises: It’s mostly relaxing by the beach, or snorkelling and diving in the Funafuti Conservation Area. You should also catch a game of “te ano”, which is commonly played on the airstrip (only when there’s no scheduled flights, of course).

There’s only one airport on the archipelago – Funafuti International – and that is only served by one airline, Fiji Airways, from Suva and Nadi in Fiji.

As for getting to Fiji, there are direct flights from Asian cities including Tokyo, Hong Kong, and Singapore, which in turn have connections from European hubs including London Heathrow, Frankfurt, Amsterdam, Brussels and Rome.

Practically speaking, you’re probably better off having Tuvalu as an add-on to a travel itinerary around Australia or New Zealand, both of which have plenty of direct flights to Fiji (then onwards to Tuvalu).

Equatorial Guinea

Located on the west coast of Africa between Cameroon and Gabon, Equatorial Guinea is the only Spanish-speaking country on the continent, having gained its independence from Spain in 1968.

As one of the largest oil producers in sub-Saharan Africa, the country hasn’t put much emphasis on tourism – according to the World Bank, international visitor arrivals are around 6,000 annually.

Those who do venture here will be rewarded with volcanic peaks and stunning waterfalls on Bioko Island, as well as an abundance of wildlife, including 16 species of primates as well as the goliath frog, the world’s largest, at Monte Alén National Park. Equatorial Guinea is also known for its nesting leatherback turtles.

The country introduced a new e-visa in 2023. It costs $75 (€68), and you’ll need to show this at the border alongside a certificate proving you have had your yellow fever vaccination.

You should also be aware that visiting many tourist sites requires permits, so it may be easier to organise your visit through a tour guide who can sort these things out for you.

The capital moved from Malabo, which is on Bioko Island, to the purpose-built Ciudad de la Paz on the mainland in January 2026.

You’ll still need to fly into Malabo, which Air France serves from Paris Charles de Gaulle. You can also fly from Frankfurt with Lufthansa, although this flight makes a stop in the Nigerian city of Lagos first.

Marshall Islands

Back to the Pacific, the Marshall Islands is perhaps more associated with its depressing nuclear history than its tourism sites, having been used by the US for testing weapons in the 40s and 50s.

In fact, the country’s only UNESCO World Heritage Site is the Bikini Atoll nuclear site, where today experienced divers can explore various wrecks including the USS Saratoga, an aircraft carrier that was sunk during testing.

Aside from diving, you can learn about traditional canoe building at Waan Aelõñ in Majel, explore World War II ruins (this time on land) in the capital Majuro or on Wotje Atoll, and relax after a day of sight-seeing by sipping on “whiskey” made from pandanus fruit.

In 2024, some 7,312 international air visitors made it to the Marshall Islands, but there are definitely efforts to attract more. In August, the tourism office launched a new pocket guide covering all the main things to do.

You can fly to the Marshall Islands on the Island Hopper route which runs from Honolulu in Hawaii to Guam, which stops off at Majuro and then Bucholz Army Airfield in the Kwajalein Atoll, before heading to Kosrae International Airport, then Pohnpei International Airport, then Chuuk International Airport, all of which are in Micronesia.

Honolulu is connected to several US cities which have direct flights from Europe, including New York, Atlanta, Dallas, San Francisco and Las Vegas.

Turkmenistan

The ‘stans of Central Asia have been getting a lot of attention in recent years, with Uzbekistan named among the fastest-growing tourism destinations for the first quarter of 2026.

One nation that perhaps isn’t getting as much love is Turkmenistan, no doubt thanks to the difficulty in obtaining a visa. The country no longer publishes its tourism numbers, but international arrivals amounted to just 8,200 people in 2007.

While a new e-visa system was rolled out at the start of October, meaning you no longer need to apply through the embassy, you still need to organise your trip through a tour agency for your permit to be approved.

Once a key part of the Silk Road, tourists can head to the UNESCO-listed oasis city of Merv, which dates back 4,000 years, as well as the Dayahatyn caravanserai near the border with Uzbekistan, which is among the best preserved throughout the region.

The capital city Ashgabat made it into the Guinness World Records book in 2013 for having the highest density of white marble-clad buildings, having been rebuilt by Turkmenistan’s first president Saparmurat Niyazov. You’ll only see white cars being driven around, too.

One thing you must not miss while visiting Turkmenistan is the Darvaza gas crater, aka the “Gates of Hell”. Continuously burning for decades, the details around how it came to be are under wraps, although there are plenty of theories.

You can fly direct to Ashgabat International Airport with Turkmenistan Airlines from Frankfurt, London Gatwick, Milan and Istanbul, as well as with Turkish Airlines from the latter.

Kiribati

Those among us who are chronically online will no doubt have heard of Kiribati thanks to the hilarious postings of @KiribatiGov on X (which, sadly, are not actually the official musings of the government), but probably won’t know anything about it.

Located in the Pacific Ocean, the archipelago of Kiribati (pronounced Kiri-bass) spans some 3,441,810 square kilometres of ocean, yet has just 811 square kilometres of land.

If you look at a map of the world, you’ll note that the International Date Line makes a major detour around Kiribati, and its furthest islands to the east are actually in the most advanced time zone, GMT+14.

Like many of the other Pacific island destinations on this list, Kiribati is known for its water-based activities, including snorkelling, diving, and saltwater fly fishing, but you can also explore World War II remnants here.

Just 9,876 people visited in 2025. If you’re ticking off the Marshall Islands on the same trip, good news, as the two are connected by Nauru Airlines.

Alternatively, you can fly here from Nadi International Airport in Fiji. We’ve already covered how to get to Fiji from Europe when writing about Tuvalu, so scroll up for that.

Niue

Another Pacific island nation (are you sensing a pattern here?), Niue is located between Tonga, Samoa and the Cook Islands, and saw just 10,210 visitors in 2019.

One for stargazers, Niue became the world’s first whole country to become an International Dark Sky Place in 2020, and you can book guided astro-tours with members of the local community who have been navigating by the stars for generations.

Again, there’s plenty of diving, snorkelling and fishing, and you can also go whale watching, either from a boat or on shore as these beautiful creatures have been known to swim incredibly close to the islands. There are also numerous hiking routes taking you to swimming spots.

The only way to reach Niue is to fly from Auckland, with Air New Zealand operating flights twice a week.

To get to Auckland, you can fly via Middle Eastern hubs like Dubai or Doha, or Asian cities like Tokyo, Seoul, Singapore, Kuala Lumpur or Bali, plus numerous Chinese cities.

Micronesia

The Federated States of Micronesia (FSM), or Micronesia for short, is made up of around 600 islands to the west of the Marshall Islands and northeast of Papua New Guinea.

It’s split into four states – Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei, and Kosrae – each of which has something different to offer tourists.

Yap, the westernmost state, is best known for its stone money, with large carved disks found throughout the island group, while Chuuk is famed for its wreck diving.

On Pohnpei, you’ll be able to see the UNESCO-listed Nan Madol, a city built more than 1,000 years ago atop around 100 islets that once served as the capital of the Saudeleur dynasty. Earlier this year, the site was named among the top 10 UNESCO World Heritage Sites by the world’s Most Travelled People.

Finally, Kosrae is also known for its ruins – both Lelu and Menke – as well as its hiking trails and diving sites.

In 2019, around 18,000 people visited Micronesia. The previously-mentioned island hopper stops at Kosrae, Pohnpei and Chuuk; there are also flights from Yap to Guam.

Solomon Islands

Emphasis on the islandS element of this country, which has more than 1,000 of them spread across Melanesia to the north east of Australia, with Fiji to the east and Micronesia to the north, although there are only six main ones.

Given its location, the Solomon Islands has much of the same things to do as some of the other spots on this list, although there are unique highlights including Kavachi, a submarine volcano nicknamed “sharkcano” for the wildlife living in its crater, and Marovo Lagoon, the largest saltwater lagoon in the world.

It’s also a great place to immerse yourself in the local culture, with many of the villages in the outer islands going without modern conveniences like electricity or internet.

You can also visit Skull Island, which is home to remains from between 300 and 1,000 years ago that were collected when headhunting was still practiced.

Official figures put the number of international visitors in 2025 at 27,329.

There are two international airports in the Solomon Islands: Honiara, which serves the capital, and Munda, in the Western Province.

The former has flights from Brisbane in Australia, as well as Nadi in Fiji, Papua New Guinea’s capital Port Moresby, and Vanuatu’s capital Port Vila; while the latter’s only international connection is Brisbane.

To get to Brisbane, you can fly via Doha or Dubai in the Middle East; or through Asian hubs like Seoul, Tokyo, Bangkok, Manila, Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, Hong Kong and Shanghai.

São Tomé and Príncipe

Leaving the Pacific Ocean behind (albeit temporarily), São Tomé and Príncipe is made up of two main islands off the northwestern coast of Gabon in central Africa.

Formed by the Cameroon volcanic line, which also created Bioko Island in Equatorial Guinea, the islands were uninhabited until being colonised by the Portuguese in the 15th century, with São Tomé and Príncipe gaining its independence in 1975.

On São Tomé, the larger of the two, you can visit the UNESCO-listed roças, aka Portuguese plantations for coffee and cocoa, or take on a two-day hike to the top of the country’s highest mountain for a view of the surrounding rainforest.

Príncipe, meanwhile, is known for the Baía das Agulhas, aka Bay of Spires, with its stunning volcanic rock towers, as well as its beaches.

A record-breaking 42,000 tourists made it to the country in 2025, according to the Portuguese news agency Lusa.

Both TAP Air Portugal and STP Airways offer direct flights from Lisbon to São Tomé, and you can fly to Príncipe on Afrijet or STP Airways.

Timor-Leste

Occupying part of the island of Timor (no points for guessing which part), as well as the exclave of Oecusse and the islands of Atauro and Jaco, Timor-Leste shares a border with Indonesia. The country’s name comes from the Malay word for east, making it the state equivalent of ordering a chai tea or paying a visit to the sahara desert.

One of the youngest countries in the world, having been occupied by Indonesia for nearly a quarter of a century, and Portugal for four centuries before that, Timor-Leste became a sovereign state in 2002.

Located in the Coral Triangle, divers headed to Ataúro Island will be able to see the greatest number of reef fish species anywhere in the world, while if you head out into the Wetar Strait and Ombai Strait between October and December, you’ll be able to go whale watching.

On land, you can hike the peak of Mount Ramelau, visit coffee plantations and support local artisans by buying tais, a traditional handwoven textile.

In 2025, 48,927 tourists visited Timor-Leste.

There are direct flights to the capital Dili from Kuala Lumpur, Bali and Xiamen, which in turn will have connections to Europe, as well as from Darwin in Australia.

Tonga

Found to the west of Niue and southeast of Fiji, Tonga is made up of more than 170 islands.

One of the best places in the world to swim with whales, the waters around the Vava’u island group are visited by the same population of humpbacks annually to mate and give birth.

Other things to do here include hiking in 'Eua National Park and paying a visit to Haʻamonga ʻa Maui, which is known as the Stonehenge of the Pacific.

In 2025, 64,183 tourists made it to Tonga.

You can fly here via Fiji’s Suva and Nadi, or from Sydney or Auckland.

Palau

The definition of small but mighty, Palau is made up of 340 islands covering some 466 square kilometres, making it the 16th smallest country in the world – yet its underwater offering is world-famous among divers.

Nicknamed the “underwater Serengeti”, popular dive sites include the UNESCO-listed Rock Islands Southern Lagoon, which has more than 385 species of coral and marine life including dugongs and 13 different types of shark, plus the Blue Corner, known for its abundance of reef sharks.

The country has put a big emphasis on protecting its natural habitats, and passports are stamped with the Palau Pledge on arrival, which visitors will need to sign, stating they promise to preserve and protect the islands.

On land, attractions include Ngardmau Waterfall, the Badrulchau Stone Monoliths, and World War II sites such as the Japanese lighthouse.

While tourism peaked in 2015 with some 168,000 visitors, a downturn in arrivals from China has meant that just 65,558 people got to experience Palau in 2025.

You can fly to Palau International Airport from Asian cities including Manila, Tokyo, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau, or from Brisbane.

Moldova

One of the least visited countries in the world can be found in our own backyard: Moldova.

In 2024, arrivals hit 67,631 – which was up 55% on the previous year, when tourist numbers were just 43,597.

Wine is the main reason to visit, with more than 200 wineries, many of which are open to the public. This includes Cricova, which has an underground wine cellar spanning some 120 kilometres, and Mileștii Mici, which has the largest wine collection in the world.

Tourists can also head to the cave monastery of Orheiul Vechi or visit Bender Fortress. Many also visit Pridnestrovian Moldovian Republic, aka Transnistria, an unrecognised breakaway state, but it should be noted that your travel insurance may be invalidated because many countries advise against visiting, including the UK’s FCDO.

There are direct flights to Chișinău Eugen Doga International Airport from all over Europe, including Amsterdam, Frankfurt, Brussels, Athens, Istanbul, London and more.

Alternatively, you can take a sleeper train from Bucharest that takes around 13 to 14 hours.

The findings should reassure pregnant women with ADHD, researchers said.

Taking ADHD medication during pregnancy does not appear to raise children's risk of autism, ADHD or other developmental issues, a major new study has found.

Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) affects an estimated 3% of adults worldwide. Most people experience a mix of inattentive, hyperactive and impulsive symptoms, which can return if they stop treatment. Even so, many pregnant women stop taking medication amid uncertainty over how the drugs may affect their developing foetuses.

The new study, published in The BMJ, set out to answer that question. It included more than 3.6 million children born from 2000 to 2021 in Sweden, Norway and Denmark. About 7,600 of these children’s mothers took ADHD medication while pregnant, including nearly 2,400 in the second or third trimester.

There was no increased risk of neurodevelopmental conditions such as ADHD, autism, intellectual disability, epilepsy or learning disorders among children with prenatal exposure to ADHD medications, the study found.

The researchers also found no increased risk tied to specific drugs, including amphetamines, methylphenidate — sold as Ritalin — and atomoxetine, sold as Strattera.

The findings should reassure women who are considering whether to keep taking their ADHD medication during pregnancy, according to the Scandinavian research team.

“Concerns about children’s future risk of neurodevelopmental disorders do not justify discontinuation of ADHD drugs in pregnancy as the results are largely reassuring,” the researchers wrote.

Children who were exposed to ADHD drugs in utero were more likely to have a neurodevelopmental disorder than children who were not exposed. However, this relationship disappeared when the researchers accounted for other factors that could play a role, such as mothers’ education, smoking habits and ADHD diagnoses.

The study has some limitations. The researchers could not account for mothers’ ADHD severity or genetics, and they tracked whether pregnant women filled their ADHD drug prescriptions, not whether they actually took their medication.

The number of children with prenatal exposure to ADHD drugs was also low, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about every medication and condition.

Still, the findings are in line with previous research that found prenatal exposure to ADHD drugs does not raise the risk of neurodevelopmental issues.

“In light of increasing use of ADHD drugs among women, our findings can aid patients and providers in their shared decisions about drug treatment of ADHD symptoms during and when planning for pregnancy,” the researchers wrote.

EU leaders will have their hands full as they wrangle over the next budget and future support for Ukraine. Both issues make for a potentially unpredictable mix.

Two of the EU's most contentious issues are set to collide at a turbulent summit in Brussels: the bloc's next long-term budget and continued support for Ukraine.

The talks on Thursday, which might stretch into Friday, aim to pave the way for a final deal at a pivotal meeting in December.

On the one hand, the 27 leaders will spar over the bloc's new long-term budget, which will determine the level of spending for critical areas like farming subsidies, infrastructure, border control and green energy for the next seven years.

António Costa, the president of the European Council, has offered a compromise that cuts the original proposal by €204 billion.

"The time has come to reach an agreement," Costa told leaders ahead of the summit.

On the other hand, they will scramble to plug Ukraine's soaring deficit and maintain a steady flow of financial and military assistance as Russia's brutal war rages on.

The European Commission has tabled a €45 billion support loan backed by joint debt to keep the country's economy afloat and its armed forces in the fight.

On paper, the two issues are separate. Politically, however, they are increasingly intertwined, creating a combustible mix that could descend into a bitter dispute.

"You can't avoid the discussions being mixed up," a diplomat said.

Stuck on red lines

The battle lines are starkly drawn.

The so-called "frugals" – Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, Sweden and Germany – are displeased with Costa's compromise and demand deeper cuts to traditional envelopes, namely agriculture and cohesion, to channel more cash into modern-day priorities such as defence, climate and technology. (Hence why they have rebranded themselves as "modernisers".)

This has met with pushback from the 17 "Friends of Cohesion", a group encompassing Southern and Eastern European countries, who want to preserve high expenditure on both traditional and modern priorities. This camp is unhappy with Costa's proposal because, they say, it cuts excessively across the board.

"I think it would have been more useful to put forward a relatively good proposal rather than playing out a bazaar scene reminiscent of Cairo, Tunis, or Marrakesh," Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said ahead of the summit.

France has adopted a hardline stance, slamming Costa's compromise as "highly disappointing", despite including the digital services tax that Paris has long advocated.

France, mired in a financial crunch at home, is keen to boost EU-wide taxes to maintain spending without increasing its national contribution.

The chasm between the competing sides has proven irreconcilable and left member states stuck on their red lines. Diplomats admit that discussions over the past few months have gone round in circles, with little meaningful progress to show for them.

The impasse puts Costa, the moderator-in-chief, in the hot seat to deliver a unanimous deal by the end of the year. The Council president intends to steer the two-day summit through bilateral and multilateral meetings to coax leaders face-to-face.

The budget is widely seen as a defining test of Costa’s presidency, with the outcome potentially weighing heavily on whether he secures a second 2.5-year term.

If negotiations spill over into 2027, they will become dangerously entangled with the French presidential election. Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner, has vowed to upend the deal and cap France's contribution at €5 billion per year.

Paris has upped the ante to avoid such a scenario.

"Several other member states will also be holding elections, beyond the French presidential election, throughout the first and even the second half of 2027," the Élysée said. "Therefore, our position has been, and remains, very clear: the negotiations cannot go beyond December."

A divisive ultimatum

Ukraine further muddles the equation.

Russia's non-stop attacks, deliberately aimed at devastating the Ukrainian economy, have drilled a €70 billion hole in Kyiv's 2027 budget.

The Commission's €45 billion loan is meant to cover two-thirds of this gap. Other allies, such as the UK, Norway, Canada and Japan, are expected to cover the remaining third.

Four member states – Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria – have already said they do not want to participate in this new loan, which will come on top of the ongoing €90 billion credit line and add to annual interest payments.

Their request has enraged German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has threatened to veto the budget if support for Ukraine is not agreed by all 27 member states. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has denounced this as a "textbook case of blackmail".

Brussels is split on whether Merz's ultimatum will succeed or backfire.

Some believe his forceful attempt to link the two files is well-founded because Russia's aggression poses a threat to the bloc as a whole.

"Security is a public good. Security is, by definition, indivisible," another senior diplomat said. "It's very difficult to understand that four countries that are getting so much cohesion funding from the EU are being so egoistic not to support the common good of security. That doesn't make sense (and) is unacceptable."

Others, however, say it is a risky manoeuvre that could alienate leaders and exacerbate mistrust. The "Friends of Cohesion" believe the optics of a deal that cuts funding for poorer regions but boosts it for Ukraine would send a politically damaging message.

The Commission has offered a way out of the showdown by allowing countries to opt in to the loan's budget strand (€20 billion) and out of its military strand (€25 billion).

Costa wants leaders to look beyond 2027 and start a serious debate on how to finance Ukraine in the longer term, whether it is a longer war or a costly recovery.

The conversation will unfold against a backdrop of a sourer, darker mood. A new poll has found 53% of Germans oppose continuing military aid for Kyiv.

Thursday's summit comes amid intense efforts to bring the peace negotiations into a multilateral format with Ukrainian, European, US and Russian officials at the same table. The Kremlin has refused to commit and instead invited the European delegation to Moscow to discuss their possible participation in the next round of talks.

Brussels thinks Russia is not yet serious about peace and has already proposed fresh economic sanctions.

A new legal study suggests Brussels could circumvent the EU’s unanimity requirement by designing a levy on oil and gas companies’ excess profits around climate or energy policy objectives rather than revenue raising.

The EU could introduce a new windfall profit tax on oil and gas companies without requiring unanimous backing from all EU countries, as long as the measure is designed primarily to advance climate or energy policy and not to raise public revenue, according to a new legal study.

The findings could potentially reopen a politically sensitive debate over who should pay for the EU's energy crises just as EU leaders gather at a summit in Brussels on Thursday and Friday to discuss the bloc's multi-annual budget for 2028-2034.

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, renewed fuel price increases and record profits for energy companies have revived calls for an EU windfall tax. The European Commission has rejected such an EU-wide tax, citing legal challenges. It ultimately reverts the matter for capitals to decide on their own.

In the study commissioned by German environmental organisations Germanwatch and Klima-Allianz Deutschland and conducted by Baldon Avocats, several possible legal routes for Brussels to impose a levy on fossil fuel companies were identified.

The legal study examines how the EU could require EU countries to introduce, collect and administer such a levy, with revenues potentially flowing either to national treasuries or the EU budget.

Avoiding unanimity

A striking finding that could pave the way for a windfall profit tax is that the Commission could potentially avoid the unanimity requirement normally associated with EU taxation by using existing treaty provisions covering environmental protection or energy policy, according to the study.

However, the tax must genuinely pursue an environmental or energy goal as its main purpose. If its main intention is to raise and redistribute money, it would be classified as a fiscal measure, triggering the unanimity requirement.

The lawyers argue that the design of the levy would be crucial.

“The label given to the instrument (‘excess profits’ or ‘windfall profits tax’, ‘solidarity contribution’) carries limited weight for the characterisation of a measure as primarily fiscal. What matters most are the aim and content of the measure,” reads the legal study.

A question of framing

A climate-focused mechanism could target profits generated specifically by fossil fuel activities, discourage further investment in polluting operations and direct revenues towards climate mitigation or adaptation.

An energy-focused version could finance energy efficiency, security of supply and measures to reduce bills for consumers.

However, framing the measure solely as a climate or energy levy would not be sufficient to bypass national vetoes. Its actual goals, tax base and allocation of revenues would determine its legal classification.

Another possibility would be to introduce the tax as part of a broader package of environmental or energy measures, with the overall purpose of the law determining its legal basis.

The 2022 precedent

The study also identifies a more immediate route akin to that used by the EU in 2022 following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

That mechanism required EU countries to impose a temporary contribution of at least 33% on exceptional profits made by companies in the crude oil, natural gas, coal and refining sectors. It applied to profits exceeding by more than 20% the average profits recorded over the previous four financial years.

Under EU law, the Council can adopt emergency economic measures by qualified majority, avoiding the need for unanimous agreement, the study noted.

The lawyers argued that a new temporary contribution could follow the same model, provided they can demonstrate exceptional circumstances and the need for emergency intervention.

The study also sees as plausible establishing a permanent EU crisis framework that could be activated temporarily whenever exceptional economic or energy circumstances arise.

However, the legal precedent is not yet settled. Energy companies have challenged the 2022 contribution before EU and national courts, questioning its legal basis and compatibility with fundamental rights.

EU Court of Justice's Advocate General, Athanasios Rantos, backed on 22 October the validity of the contribution under EU law. The Court of Justice is expected to deliver its ruling in 2027.

Who gets the money?

Beyond whether the tax can be introduced, who gets the money could become another major political battleground.

The study proposes allowing revenues to remain in national budgets while restricting their use through EU legislation, using the revenues to create a new EU budget own resource, or assigning the proceeds to a dedicated European fund.

The first option would broadly replicate the 2022 arrangement, giving national governments control over collection while requiring spending to follow goals established by EU law.

The second would be more complicated, according to the lawyers. Establishing a new EU own resource requires unanimous approval by EU countries and ratification at the national level, potentially bringing back the very veto problem that supporters of the tax would seek to avoid.

But the third option could provide an alternative. The lawyers argued that revenues could be assigned to a dedicated EU fund through secondary legislation without creating a new own resource.

Spain's proposal for a European Climate Resilience Levy on fossil fuel profits, with revenues directed towards a dedicated Climate Adaptation Fund, is one example flagged in the study.

The lawyers stress that the mechanism would require national authorities to levy and collect the tax. Direct collection by the EU itself would be difficult under the existing treaties.

EU member states are discussing a package of new Europe-wide taxes to finance the bloc's next long-term budget. But where is the money coming from? Euronews provides an overview of who will pay for each new levy.

EU leaders are engaged in intense discussion over the bloc's new seven-year budget before the end of the year, with member states butting heads over the overall size, spending priorities and how to finance it.

In terms of new resources Brussels intends to tap into, European Council President Antonio Costa proposed an ambitious mix of EU-wide taxes meant to generate about €60bn in revenue each year.

But who pays the bill? With Costa's compromise, the European Commission circulated an updated estimate of how much each Europe-wide tax is meant to generate, and which countries will bear most of the costs.

Between 2028 and 2034, Germany would be by far the country paying the highest share of EU taxes, with over €13bn in current prices, followed by Italy with €8bn. Despite being the bloc's second-largest economy, France merely ranks third, which explains Paris' strong support for new own resources.

However, the asymmetrical contribution to own resources is best understood in terms of what they would otherwise pay in national contributions based on their Gross National Income (GNI).

Costa's proposal made several adjustments to the EU taxes, mostly to accommodate objections from member states from central and eastern Europe, leaving southern European countries to pay the highest share.

On average, the tax of €2.25 per kilogram of uncollected electronic waste is by far the one expected to yield more revenues, with over €20bn expected per year, despite it being relatively less controversial than the Emissions Trading System (ETS), the Tobacco Tax or the digital levy.

While the e-waste contribution is the largest for most member states, how much each own resource will weigh on the national governments varies considerably, shaping the positioning of the member states.

The revenues expected from each tax are not fixed due to a number of reasons, including the fact that several of them will be adjusted for inflation.

The Commission projects the yields might significantly increase over time, with the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a tax on imports of carbon-intensive products, expected to more than double its revenues by 2034.

For the tax of €1.25 per kilogram of non-recycled plastic packaging waste, over half of the revenues are expected to come from the EU's four largest member states, France, Germany, Italy and Spain.

Similarly, the four EU countries would also account for over 60% of the revenues coming from an EU-wide digital services tax. France, Italy and Spain already have a digital levy at the national level, meaning they would lose these revenues in favour of Brussels.

The yields of the tobacco excise duty are also highly geographically concentrated, but in this case there is a less linear relation with the member states' population and reflects more national consumption habits and national excise duty levels.

Luxembourg, for instance, would make a significant contribution despite its relatively tiny size, as it sells large volumes of cigarettes and related products to consumers from neighbouring countries thanks to its lower prices.

For the tax on e-waste, which envisages a contribution from member states based on the share of electronic devices produced on their territory that are recycled, over 60% of the revenues would come from Germany, Italy and France, the EU's manufacturing powerhouses. By contrast, the Commission estimates Bulgaria would have to pay zero.

Giving 30% of the revenues generated from the Emissions Trading System (ETS), a carbon market for CO2-intensive industries, would be particularly advantageous for France, which would be in fourth position in terms of contribution, whilst it would penalise countries like Poland and Bulgaria compared to their economic size.

Italy would be the first payer for the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), with Belgium and Poland also punching above their weight in terms of contributions.
